patient.chief_complaint: Sudden onset left-sided weakness and not using the left side of the body
patient.history_present_illness: Mrs. Dorothy Harrington is a 74-year-old right-handed woman with a history of hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and diet-controlled type 2 diabetes who was brought to the emergency department by her daughter after sudden onset of left-sided weakness and behavioral change. The daughter reports she called her mother at approximately 09:00 this morning and she sounded entirely normal. She arrived at her mother's home at 11:20 for a planned visit and found her sitting in the kitchen chair unable to rise, with her left arm hanging limply at her side and appearing oblivious to objects and people on her left side. The patient denied anything was wrong when asked, attributing her inability to stand to her bad knees. The daughter called 911 immediately. EMS arrived at 11:34 and documented left hemiplegia, apparent neglect of the left side, and rightward gaze preference. A stroke alert was activated in the field. Blood glucose obtained by EMS was 128 mg/dL. The patient arrived in the emergency department at 11:58. Last known well time is established at 09:00, approximately 2 hours and 58 minutes before ED arrival, placing her within the standard IV alteplase window. On cardiac monitoring in the ED, the rhythm appeared irregularly irregular, prompting an urgent 12-lead ECG. The patient is unable to reliably report symptom onset; she demonstrates apparent anosognosia for her left-sided deficits. She denies headache, nausea, vomiting, or loss of consciousness. She reports no recent chest pain, fever, or illness. Her medications include amlodipine, lisinopril, atorvastatin, and aspirin 81 mg daily. She has not taken any anticoagulants. Her blood pressure on arrival is 188/104 mmHg, which she and her daughter attribute to her chronic hypertension. The daughter confirms her mother has never been diagnosed with atrial fibrillation and has not seen a cardiologist in several years.

results.title: 2019 AHA/ASA Guidelines for the Early Management of Acute Ischemic Stroke
results.authors: Powers WJ, Rabinstein AA, Ackerson T, et al.
results.key_finding: IV alteplase 0.9 mg/kg is recommended within 4.5 hours of last known well in eligible patients. Blood pressure must be reduced to <185/110 mmHg before tPA administration. Mechanical thrombectomy is recommended for LVO (ICA or MCA M1) within 24 hours using DAWN/DEFUSE-3 criteria.

results.title: Thrombectomy 6-24 hours after stroke with a mismatch between deficit and infarct (DAWN)
results.authors: Nogueira RG, Jadhav AP, Haussen DC, et al.
results.key_finding: In patients with LVO presenting 6-24 hours after last known well with clinical-core mismatch, thrombectomy led to better functional outcomes at 90 days versus standard care.

results.title: Thrombectomy for Stroke at 6 to 16 Hours (DEFUSE 3)
results.authors: Albers GW, Marks MP, Kemp S, et al.
results.key_finding: Thrombectomy in patients with LVO 6-16 hours after symptom onset selected by perfusion imaging mismatch criteria significantly improved functional outcomes.

results.title: TOAST Classification of Stroke Subtypes
results.authors: Adams HP Jr, Bendixen BH, Kappelle LJ, et al.
results.key_finding: TOAST classification categorizes ischemic stroke into large-artery atherosclerosis, cardioembolism, small-vessel occlusion, other determined etiology, and undetermined. Cardioembolic strokes are associated with cardiac sources including atrial fibrillation.

output.summary: IV alteplase (0.9 mg/kg, max 90 mg) is the standard of care for eligible acute ischemic stroke patients within 4.5 hours of last known well. Key inclusion criteria include measurable neurological deficit and exclusion of hemorrhage on imaging. Key absolute contraindications include active internal bleeding, recent intracranial surgery, and prior ICH. Blood pressure must be controlled to <185/110 mmHg before tPA. For large vessel occlusion, mechanical thrombectomy is recommended up to 24 hours in selected patients meeting DAWN or DEFUSE-3 criteria. TOAST classification identifies cardioembolic mechanism (atrial fibrillation, cardiac thrombus) as a major stroke subtype requiring anticoagulation for secondary prevention.

output.proposed: Alteplase (tPA) 0.9 mg/kg IV and subsequent anticoagulation (DOAC) for atrial fibrillation
interactions: Aspirin 81 mg daily: Aspirin is not a contraindication to IV alteplase per AHA/ASA guidelines. Antiplatelet therapy should be held for 24 hours after alteplase administration.
Lisinopril (ACE inhibitor): ACE inhibitors may increase risk of orolingual angioedema after alteplase administration. Monitor closely for tongue and lip swelling during and after infusion.
Atorvastatin: No direct interaction with alteplase. Continue statin for secondary prevention.
contraindications: No current anticoagulant use — INR 1.0, PTT normal; no contraindication from anticoagulation status
No recent major surgery or trauma reported
Blood pressure must be reduced to <185/110 mmHg before initiating alteplase
warnings: Lisinopril: Monitor for ACE-inhibitor-associated orolingual angioedema post-tPA — occurs in approximately 1-5% of cases, more common with ACE inhibitor use
Blood pressure on arrival 188/104 mmHg — exceeds pre-tPA threshold of 185/110 mmHg; antihypertensive treatment required before alteplase initiation
After alteplase, avoid anticoagulation and antiplatelet agents for 24 hours

Subsequent anticoagulation for AF-related cardioembolic stroke: DOAC preferred over warfarin for non-valvular AF; timing of initiation post-stroke depends on infarct size and hemorrhagic transformation risk
alternatives: Tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg IV single bolus — non-inferior to alteplase per AcT trial; simpler administration particularly in bridging-to-thrombectomy setting
Apixaban 5 mg BID or rivaroxaban 20 mg daily for AF secondary prevention (DOACs preferred over warfarin for non-valvular AF per AHA/ASA guidelines)

sequence_constraints.reason: Non-contrast head CT must exclude intracranial hemorrhage before IV thrombolysis (tPA contraindication check) is relevant.
Glucose, INR/PTT, and platelet count must be available to exclude hypoglycemia mimic and coagulopathy contraindications before tPA decision.

critical_actions: Establish time of last known well (LKW — 09:00, approximately 3 hours before ED arrival) and calculate NIHSS to confirm acute treatment eligibility
Obtain non-contrast CT head FIRST to exclude intracranial hemorrhage before any thrombolytic decision
Lower blood pressure to <185/110 mmHg before IV alteplase administration (arrival BP 188/104 mmHg marginally exceeds threshold)
Administer IV alteplase 0.9 mg/kg (or tenecteplase) within the 4.5-hour window if no contraindications — patient is within window
Proceed immediately to mechanical thrombectomy evaluation given right MCA M1 occlusion on CTA (LVO — thrombectomy eligible up to 24h per DAWN/DEFUSE-3)
Monitor closely for orolingual angioedema during and after tPA infusion (patient on lisinopril, ACE inhibitor increases this risk)
Verify glucose to exclude hypoglycemia as a stroke mimic (glucose mildly elevated, not hypoglycemic)
Initiate continuous telemetry throughout hospitalization; document AF burden on cardiac monitoring
Initiate anticoagulation with a DOAC for AF-related secondary stroke prevention at appropriate interval after infarct (timing based on infarct size and hemorrhagic transformation risk)
Do NOT aggressively lower blood pressure beyond the pre-tPA threshold — post-tPA target <180/105 mmHg for 24 hours; outside tPA window maintain permissive hypertension
contraindicated_actions: Do not administer IV tPA before non-contrast CT excludes intracranial hemorrhage
Do not give IV tPA if blood pressure remains above 185/110 mmHg after antihypertensive treatment
Do not give IV tPA if INR >1.7, platelet count <100,000, or other guideline-listed absolute contraindications are present
Do not aggressively lower blood pressure below 140/90 mmHg in the acute phase — risks worsening ischemic penumbra perfusion
Do not delay non-contrast CT to obtain additional history or labs in a stroke alert presentation
Do not rely on aspirin alone for secondary prevention in confirmed AF-related cardioembolic stroke — oral anticoagulation (DOAC) is required
Do not start full anticoagulation in the acute phase without considering hemorrhagic transformation risk for a large-territory infarct
key_reasoning_points: RIGHT MCA territory infarct produces LEFT-sided hemiparesis, LEFT-sided sensory loss, and LEFT hemineglect — the cortical gaze preference deviates RIGHTWARD (toward the lesion, away from the side of deficit); there is NO aphasia because the right hemisphere is non-dominant in this right-handed patient

Atrial fibrillation on initial ECG combined with large-territory cortical infarct and right MCA M1 occlusion on CTA establishes cardioembolic mechanism by TOAST classification; bilateral carotid duplex <30% stenosis excludes large-artery atherosclerosis as the competing mechanism
Time of last known well of approximately 3 hours places this patient within the standard IV alteplase window (<=4.5h); right MCA M1 LVO on CTA additionally opens the mechanical thrombectomy pathway

Elevated arrival blood pressure (188/104 mmHg) is expected with acute stroke from autoregulatory changes — do NOT lower aggressively; reduce only to <185/110 mmHg if IV tPA is planned, then maintain <180/105 mmHg for 24 hours post-tPA
Lisinopril (ACE inhibitor) combined with tPA increases risk of orolingual angioedema approximately 2-5 fold — requires close monitoring during and after infusion
Anosognosia (denial of left-sided deficit) is a classic feature of right hemisphere non-dominant lesions and should not be mistaken for psychiatric behavior or drug effect
